title.narrative: Innovation for Indonesia's School Children (INOVASI) Phase 3

description.narrative: The INOVASI Phase 3 program builds on the work, and lessons learned, from previous phases which focused on improving students’ foundational skills, particularly literacy, numeracy, and character education. INOVASI is an adaptive program which trials, learns from and improves collective and localised system approaches in implementing relevant education policies and reforms by working in five educational levers. These include curriculum and assessment, teaching practices, school leadership, GEDSI, and climate resilience. INOVASI continues to work in East Java, North Kalimantan, West Nusa Tenggara, and East Nusa Tenggara provinces. In this phase, INOVASI has expanded to additional provinces—Maluku, West Java, and the Capital City of Nusantara—making it six provinces in total. INOVASI has also widened the scope from early grades to one-year pre-primary until sixth grade of primary school.

description.narrative: INOVASI contributed to improved student performance in literacy and numeracy across 11 partner districts, as evidenced in the 2025 national Indonesian education report. This was through technical assistance, teacher training, piloting local innovations, and policy advocacy. ‍ In Nagekeo (East Nusa Tenggara), literacy proficiency rose from 65% (2023) to 79.7% (2025), and numeracy to 74.7%, surpassing the national 70% benchmark. INOVASI supported the use of mother tongue in early grades and piloted a language transition model, with a local teacher training institute, which later adopted this into their curriculum. ‍ In Tarakan (North Kalimantan), INOVASI supported literacy efforts and piloted anti-violence school modules, resulting in a literacy minimum proficiency rate of 79.8% and 70.6% numeracy. ‍ In Bulungan (North Kalimantan province), literacy improved from 58.5% to 69.8%, and numeracy from 41.5% to 63.2%. INOVASI facilitated the use of local government funds for quality reading books and implement a system to identify learning difficulties. This enabled targeted teaching and support. ‍ Seven districts exceeded the national average gain in literacy, and six in numeracy. These results reflect INOVASI’s locally driven, effective strategies that benefit thousands of both teachers and students.

INOVASI is working with HWDI East Lombok (West Nusa Tenggara) to improve inclusive education and prevent gender-based violence in schools. In June, 2025, HWDI visited 9 schools to check how ready they were to support students with disabilities and handle violence cases. INOVASI facilitators joined the visits. The team found that while most schools had school-based violence response teams (TPPKs), many teachers lacked proper training on disability inclusion and violence prevention. ‍ HWDI then adapted modules from the Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education and shared clear, practical guides with teachers, school supervisors, and students. They also ran community awareness events for parents and helped connect TPPKs with the Lombok Timur district task force. These activities reached around 14 schools, more than 50 educators, and hundreds of community members. ‍ Local government gave strong support as this work aligns with the 2024 Education Planning Process—which made inclusive education a district priority. HWDI’s work also helped build skills of at least five other OPDs, including LIDI, Pertuni, and PPDI. ‍ This matters because it improves both access and safety for children with disabilities and shows how local disability groups can lead meaningful change.

INOVASI partnered with HWDI, an NGO focused on inclusive education in Sidoarjo (East Java), to help create more inclusive and safe school environments. In June 2025, HWDI held a training session with 37 participants, including 26 women (6 with physical disabilities) and 11 men (1 visually impaired). Attendees included teachers, principals, education officials, and civil society groups like LPKIPI. ‍ The group discussed key challenges, including a lack of Special Education Teachers (GPK). With just one GPK for every 15 students with learning difficulties, the district proposed hiring more teachers in phases. HWDI helped bring attention to the voices of people with disabilities and their families, and supported the recognition of disability groups like Pertuni, and Gerkatin. ‍ Following the session, stakeholders agreed to work together through a new Inclusion Working Group. The District Education Office committed to running district-wide campaigns to raise disability awareness. Schools also began making plans to improve inclusive practices, extending efforts beyond the original 5–10 targeted schools and 30 teachers. ‍ This work helps strengthen the role of disability groups in shaping local education plans and policies. HWDI’s efforts show how collaboration between community groups and government can lead to long-term improvements in inclusive education.

INOVASI partnered with Yayasan Wahana Inklusif Indonesia (Wahana), an inclusive education focused NGO, to strengthen inclusive practices in Cirebon, West Java. This was to promote the establishment of disability service units to better support students with disabilities. Wahana engaged 50 participants—including 14 Organisation for People with Disabilities (OPD) representatives and 15 government stakeholders—in a workshop introducing inclusive education initiatives. Of these, 16 were women (including 2 blind participants) and 34 were men (7 with disabilities, including physical, visual, and hearing impairments). Government agencies committed to allocating funds in the next fiscal year to improve teacher capacity on disability inclusion. ‍ On June 14, 2025, Wahana hosted a follow-up event with 16 participants from 8 disability organisations and working groups (e.g., HWDI, PPDI, Gerkatin, PERTUNI), including 9 people with disabilities. This initiative strengthened collaboration among OPDs, parents, and communities to support inclusive education. ‍ The partnership has extended capacity-building support to at least five more OPDs, expanding INOVASI’s reach beyond Wahana. These early efforts have started sparked policy dialogue, improved inter-agency coordination, and built OPD capacities in advocacy, M&E, and delivering reasonable accommodations. Wahana’s work supports national inclusive education mandates and offers a replicable model for disability service unit development in other districts.
